title: Choosing keys and partition counts
summary: Pick the key that defines your ordered lane, spot hot keys and skew, size the partition count from throughput, and avoid the C#/Java partitioner mismatch and the remap that adding partitions causes.

steps.title: The key decides the partition
body: For a keyed record the producer computes `partition = hash(key) % partitionCount`. Same key, same hash, same
partition, same order. Choosing the key is choosing **what stays in order** and **how the load spreads**:
```text
key = orderId           A1 A1 A1 | B7 B7 | C4 ...     many keys, even spread, per-order order     (usual choice)
key = customerId        all orders of one customer in order          good when a customer's events interact
key = tenantId          tenant-7 = 70% of traffic -> one hot partition, one overloaded consumer   (skew)
key = null              sticky partitioner: fill a batch for one partition, then switch          no order at all
key = "orders"          everything on one partition: global order, zero parallelism
- Use the id of the **entity whose events must stay ordered**: usually the aggregate id (order, account, device).
- Watch for **hot keys**: one huge tenant or a default value like `"unknown"` or `""` puts a big share of the traffic
on one partition, and lag grows on that one partition only.
- A partition holds many keys; you only need their **events per key** in order, not the partition as a whole.
- Never use `string.GetHashCode()` for routing in .NET: it is **randomised per process**, so every restart sends
the same key somewhere else.
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *Same key, same partition*.

steps.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS keys `invoice-events` by `tenantId`. Tenant `northwind` produces 70% of all events. What will on-call see?
options: One partition with growing lag and one consumer at full CPU while the others idle; adding consumers does not help
Evenly spread lag, fixed by adding consumers
Kafka rebalances the hot key across partitions automatically
Producer errors, because a key may only use 10% of a topic
explain: All of one tenant's records land on one partition, and one partition is consumed by one group member: that is your
throughput ceiling for that tenant. Options: a finer key (`tenantId:invoiceId`) when per-invoice order is enough, or a
dedicated topic for the big tenant. Kafka never splits a key across partitions.

steps.title: Fix the partitioner that moves keys on every deploy
prompt: **Bug report:** after each deploy of orders-api, events of the same order land on a **different partition** than before
the deploy, the Java stock service disagrees with us about where an order lives, and once a week a send fails with
`System.OverflowException: Negating the minimum value of a twos complement number is invalid`.
The code below routes with `key.GetHashCode()` (randomised per process in .NET) and `Math.Abs` (which throws for
`int.MinValue`). Fix `int PartitionFor(string key, int partitions)` so it does what the Java client does:
`Murmur2` is given and correct. The `& 0x7fffffff` clears the sign bit, which is how Kafka makes the hash positive
starter: // Kafka's murmur2 (org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.murmur2), given: do not change it
solution: // Kafka's murmur2 (org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.murmur2), given: do not change it
template: Dojo.Eq("Murmur2 is intact (Kafka's own test vector)", -973932308, Murmur2(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("21")));
Dojo.Eq("A1 goes to partition 3 of 6, like the Java client", 3, PartitionFor("A1", 6));
Dojo.Eq("B7 goes to partition 4 of 6, like the Java client", 4, PartitionFor("B7", 6));
Dojo.Eq("order-1042 goes to partition 0 of 6, like the Java client", 0, PartitionFor("order-1042", 6));
Dojo.Eq("tenant-7 goes to partition 0 of 6, like the Java client", 0, PartitionFor("tenant-7", 6));
Dojo.Eq("C4 goes to partition 2 of 6, like the Java client", 2, PartitionFor("C4", 6));

steps.title: Two clients, two partitioners
body: The hash is part of the contract between **every producer of a topic** (and Kafka Streams or Flink jobs that join
topics by key). The clients do **not** agree by default:
| Client | Default for keyed records | Null keys |
| Java (also Kafka Streams, Spring Kafka, the console producer) | murmur2 | sticky partitioner |
| librdkafka: Confluent.Kafka (.NET), confluent-kafka-python, Go | `consistent_random`: **CRC32** of the key | random, made sticky by `sticky.partitioning.linger.ms` |
So a C# producer and a Java producer writing `A1` to the same topic can put it on **different partitions**: events of
one order on two partitions, consumed by two members, in no particular order. Make .NET match Java:
```csharp fragment
var pc = new ProducerConfig
BootstrapServers = "kafka:9092",
Partitioner = Partitioner.Murmur2Random,   // murmur2 for keys like Java, random (sticky) for null keys
EnableIdempotence = true,
Do it on day one: changing the partitioner of an existing topic moves keys, exactly like adding partitions does.

steps.prompt: A C# service starts producing to a topic that Java services already write to, keyed by `orderId`. Complete the config.
code: using var producer = new ProducerBuilder<string, string>(pc).Build();
await producer.ProduceAsync("order-events", new Message<string, string> { Key = __3__, Value = json });
explain: `Murmur2Random` matches the Java client for keyed records; `ConsistentRandom` (the librdkafka default) uses CRC32 and
disagrees. The key must be the entity id: a `null` key gives up ordering entirely.

steps.title: How many partitions?
body: Size the partition count from **throughput** and **parallelism**, with room to grow:
```text
target 60 MB/s  ·  one partition sustains ~20 MB/s produce  ·  one consumer handles ~5 MB/s
partitions >= max( 60 / 20 , 60 / 5 , planned consumers ) = max( 3, 12, 6 ) = 12
- The slowest side wins, and it is usually the **consumer** (your handler calls a database).
- A group can use at most **one consumer per partition**: the count is the ceiling on parallelism.
- **Adding partitions remaps keys.** `hash % 6` and `hash % 8` differ for most keys, so after
`kafka-topics.sh --alter --topic orders --partitions 8` new events of order A1 may land on a new partition while
its old events are still being processed from the old one: a window of out-of-order processing. You **cannot**
reduce the count at all. So pick a count with headroom (for example 2-3 times today's need) at creation time.
- Too many partitions cost too: more files and memory per broker, longer leader elections, more consumer overhead.
KRaft clusters handle far more partitions than the ZooKeeper era, but hundreds per topic still need a reason.
If you must grow a keyed topic: pause producers or drain consumers before `--alter`, or create a new topic with the
right count and migrate.

steps.prompt: Which question does each command answer?
buckets: Plan or change the partition count

steps.title: Plan the partitions
prompt: Write the planning helpers you would use before creating or growing a topic. `Murmur2` is given.
- `int PartitionFor(string key, int partitions)`: the Java-compatible partitioner from the bug fix.
- `int PartitionsFor(double targetMBps, double producerMBpsPerPartition, double consumerMBpsPerPartition, int plannedConsumers)`:
the largest of `ceil(target / producerPerPartition)`, `ceil(target / consumerPerPartition)` and `plannedConsumers`.
- `double MovedFraction(IEnumerable<string> keys, int from, int to)`: the share of keys whose partition changes when the
count goes from `from` to `to` (0 for no keys).
starter: // Kafka's murmur2 (org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.murmur2), given: do not change it
int PartitionsFor(double targetMBps, double producerMBpsPerPartition, double consumerMBpsPerPartition, int plannedConsumers)
double MovedFraction(IEnumerable<string> keys, int from, int to)
solution: // Kafka's murmur2 (org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.murmur2), given: do not change it
int PartitionsFor(double targetMBps, double producerMBpsPerPartition, double consumerMBpsPerPartition, int plannedConsumers)
double MovedFraction(IEnumerable<string> keys, int from, int to)
return (double)list.Count(k => PartitionFor(k, from) != PartitionFor(k, to)) / list.Count;
hints: `(int)Math.Ceiling(target / perPartition)` for each side, then `Math.Max` of the three.
`MovedFraction`: count the keys with `PartitionFor(k, from) != PartitionFor(k, to)` and divide by the count as a `double`.
template: Dojo.Eq("planned consumers can be the largest", 6, PartitionsFor(10, 10, 10, 6));
